 "id":"Q35",
 "sourceFile":"The return to sport clearance continuum is a novel approach toward return to sport and performance for the professional athlete.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title 'The Return-to-Sport Clearance Continuum Is a Novel Approach Toward Return to Sport and Performance for the Professional Athlete' in the text matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain":"Rehabilitation & Return to Sport",
 "domains":["Rehabilitation & Return to Sport","Sports Medicine & Injury","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Rehabilitation","Sports Medicine","Performance","Athletic Training"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Professional / Elite","Injured Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Expert-opinion clinical review (Level V, as the authors state) that proposes the Return to Sport Clearance Continuum, a five-phase framework running from repair through rehabilitation, reconditioning and performance to training camp and preseason, with criterion-based testing and load monitoring throughout. It summarises common return-to-sport tests for lower-extremity injuries, including strength and limb symmetry, hop, balance, movement quality and force-plate measures. No sample, outcome data or validation of the continuum is presented.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The framework is an opinion proposal with no data from its own use, so its effect on return to sport or performance is untested. No literature search method is described, and the cited evidence is mostly lower-extremity injury work, largely in professional athletes.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could treat the continuum as a validated clearance protocol and read the cited thresholds, such as limb symmetry above 85% or the 4 cm Y-balance difference, as universal pass marks.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2022,
   "citation":"Draovitch P, Patel S, Marrone W, et al. The return-to-sport clearance continuum is a novel approach toward return to sport and performance for the professional athlete. Arthroscopy, Sports Medicine, and Rehabilitation. 2022;4(1):e93-e101.",
   "doi":"10.1016/j.asmr.2021.10.026",
   "abstract":"The authors argue that return to sport for professional athletes should be an evolving continuum of criterion-based checks, not a single decision at one point in time. The article presents the Return to Sport Clearance Continuum with five phases and describes progressive, regular qualitative and quantitative testing to help athletes return at their maximal performance level. The level of evidence is V, expert opinion.",
   "tldr":"The authors propose the Return to Sport Clearance Continuum, which treats return to sport as a series of criterion-based checkpoints with regular testing and load monitoring. It is a proposed framework that has not been tested against outcomes.",
   "methods":"Expert-opinion clinical review. The authors describe a five-phase continuum and summarise common return-to-sport tests (strength and limb symmetry, hop, balance, qualitative movement and force-plate measures) for lower-extremity injuries. No literature search method is described.",
   "findings":"The authors present return to sport as criterion-based and continuous rather than time-based. They cite studies linking objective criteria or longer delays before return with lower reinjury rates, and note that limb symmetry indices can overestimate knee function. The continuum itself was not tested in data.",
   "limitations":"The framework is expert opinion (Level V) with no sample, no outcome data and no validity or reliability testing of the continuum. The authors acknowledge that 3D motion analysis and force plates are not available in every setting. The evidence cited is drawn mainly from lower-extremity injury studies, largely in professional athletes.",
   "practicalImplications":"Use a set of checkpoints across the recovery process, with both quantitative and qualitative tests, instead of relying on a single clearance test or on time since injury. Share the current phase and its criteria across the physician, therapist, strength coach and athlete so that expectations match.",
   "athleteDev":"After return, the paper recommends a preseason plan that manages loads, repetitions and days off, with load monitoring continuing through the season. It also notes that success in the first year after injury does not guarantee success later, and that joint health after ACL reconstruction may take up to 2 years to return to baseline.",
   "rtp":"The framework supports progressing athletes through phases on criteria rather than time alone, with strength, hop, balance and movement testing at each stage. It does not give validated pass thresholds or a clearance rule, so it cannot make a return-to-play decision on its own."
 }
}

 "evidenceSummary":"Expert-opinion clinical review (Level V, as the authors state) that proposes the Return to Sport Clearance Continuum, a five-phase framework running from repair through rehabilitation, reconditioning and performance to training camp and preseason, with criterion-based testing and load monitoring throughout. It summarises common return-to-sport tests for lower-extremity injuries, including strength and limb symmetry, hop, balance, movement quality and force-plate measures. No sample, outcome data or validation of the continuum is presented.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The framework is an opinion proposal with no data from its own use, so its effect on return to sport or performance is untested. No literature search method is described, and the cited evidence is mostly lower-extremity injury work, largely in professional athletes.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could treat the continuum as a validated clearance protocol and read the cited thresholds, such as limb symmetry above 85% or the 4 cm Y-balance difference, as universal pass marks.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2022,

   "doi":"10.1016/j.asmr.2021.10.026",
   "abstract":"The authors argue that return to sport for professional athletes should be an evolving continuum of criterion-based checks, not a single decision at one point in time. The level of evidence is V, expert opinion.",
   "tldr":"The authors propose the Return to Sport Clearance Continuum, which treats return to sport as a series of criterion-based checkpoints with regular testing and load monitoring. It is a proposed framework that has not been tested against outcomes.",
   "methods":"Expert-opinion clinical review. The authors describe a five-phase continuum and summarise common return-to-sport tests (strength and limb symmetry, hop, balance, qualitative movement and force-plate measures) for lower-extremity injuries. No literature search method is described.",
   "findings":"The authors present return to sport as criterion-based and continuous rather than time-based. They cite studies linking objective criteria or longer delays before return with lower reinjury rates, and note that limb symmetry indices can overestimate knee function. The continuum itself was not tested in data.",
   "limitations":"The framework is expert opinion (Level V) with no sample, no outcome data and no validity or reliability testing of the continuum. The authors acknowledge that 3D motion analysis and force plates are not available in every setting. Abstract: The concept of returning to sport for a professional athlete is still under debate for the professional athlete in
today’s sports environment. It is critical for the professional athlete to be able to return to sport at a highly competitive
level but also to return in a safe and timely measure. With no “gold standard” of sport testing, it is difﬁcult to determine
what the right progression or testing regimen should be. The Return to Sport Clearance Continuum does not look at one
moment in time, but looks throughout the continuum of healing to determine readiness for sport. The purpose of this
article is to explore the concept of RTS being part of an evolving continuum rather than the traditional notion that RTS is a
single decision made at a discrete point in time. The principles of progressive but regular testing procedures including
qualitative and quantitative movement are presented to help the professional athlete return to sport at their maximal
performance level. Level of Evidence: V, expert opinion.

 "primaryDomain":"Rehabilitation & Return to Sport",

 "audiences":["Rehabilitation","Sports Medicine","Performance","Athletic Training"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Professional / Elite","Injured Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Expert-opinion clinical review (Level V, as the authors state) that proposes the Return to Sport Clearance Continuum, a five-phase framework running from repair through rehabilitation, reconditioning and performance to training camp and preseason, with criterion-based testing and load monitoring throughout. It summarises common return-to-sport tests for lower-extremity injuries, including strength and limb symmetry, hop, balance, movement quality and force-plate measures. No sample, outcome data or validation of the continuum is presented.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The framework is an opinion proposal with no data from its own use, so its effect on return to sport or performance is untested. No literature search method is described, and the cited evidence is mostly lower-extremity injury work, much of it on ACL reconstruction.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could treat the continuum as a validated clearance protocol and read the cited thresholds, such as limb symmetry above 85% or the 4 cm Y-balance difference, as universal pass marks.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2022,
   "citation":"Draovitch P, Patel S, Marrone W, Grundstein MJ, Grant R, Virgile A, et al. The return-to-sport clearance continuum is a novel approach toward return to sport and performance for the professional athlete. Arthroscopy, Sports Medicine, and Rehabilitation. 2022;4(1):e93-e101.",
   "doi":"10.1016/j.asmr.2021.10.026",
   "abstract":"The authors argue that return to sport for professional athletes should be an evolving continuum of criterion-based checks, not a single decision at one point in time. The article presents the Return to Sport Clearance Continuum with five phases and describes progressive, regular qualitative and quantitative testing to help athletes return at their maximal performance level. The level of evidence is V, expert opinion.",
   "tldr":"The authors propose the Return to Sport Clearance Continuum, which treats return to sport as a series of criterion-based checkpoints with regular testing and load monitoring. It is a proposed framework that has not been tested against outcomes.",
   "methods":"Expert-opinion clinical review. The authors describe a five-phase continuum and summarise common return-to-sport tests (strength and limb symmetry, hop, balance, qualitative movement and force-plate measures) for lower-extremity injuries. No literature search method is described.",
   "findings":"The authors present return to sport as criterion-based and continuous rather than time-based. They cite studies linking objective criteria or longer delays before return with lower reinjury rates, and note that limb symmetry indices can overestimate knee function. The continuum itself was not tested in data.",
   "limitations":"The framework is expert opinion (Level V) with no sample, no outcome data and no validity or reliability testing of the continuum. The authors note that the extent of movement analysis will vary with institutional resources such as 3D motion analysis and force plates. The evidence cited is drawn mainly from lower-extremity injury studies, especially ACL reconstruction.",
   "practicalImplications":"Use a set of checkpoints across the recovery process, with both quantitative and qualitative tests, instead of relying on a single clearance test or on time since injury. Share the current phase and its criteria across the physician, therapist, strength coach and athlete so that expectations match.",
   "athleteDev":"After return, the paper recommends a preseason plan that manages loads, repetitions and days off, with load monitoring continuing through the season. It also notes that success in the first year after injury does not guarantee success later, and that joint health after ACL reconstruction may take up to 2 years to return to baseline.",
   "rtp":"The framework supports progressing athletes through phases on criteria rather than time alone, with strength, hop, balance and movement testing at each stage. It does not give validated pass thresholds or a clearance rule, so it cannot make a return-to-play decision on its own."

     "paper.limitations: 'not available in every setting' reworded to the source wording ('will vary based on institutional resource availability')"

   "residualConcerns":"",
   "spotCheckPriority":"high"
 }

 "id":"Q36",
 "sourceFile":"The risk of all-cause injury and site-specific injury in athletes after concussion - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title 'The risk of all-cause injury and site-specific injury in athletes after concussion: a systematic review and meta-analysis' in the text matches the filename; the text is an unedited accepted manuscript (article in press).",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury","Rehabilitation & Return to Sport","Brain Health & Psychology"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Rehabilitation","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Professional / Elite","Collegiate","Youth / Adolescent","Injured Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of 19 cohort studies covering 86,879 athletes, comparing athletes with and without a prior sport-related concussion. Prior concussion was associated with higher odds of subsequent all-cause injury (OR 1.93, 95% CI 1.39 to 2.68), recurrent concussion (OR 3.06, 95% CI 1.81 to 5.17), upper-extremity injury (OR 1.76, two studies) and lower-extremity injury (OR 1.49, nine studies). Heterogeneity was high for all-cause injury (I2 = 94.4%).",
 "screeningLimitations":"The included studies are observational cohorts, five of them unadjusted, and heterogeneity was high, so the pooled odds ratios are averages across varied settings rather than risks for an individual athlete. The follow-up-duration moderator was not significant in meta-regression (p = 0.629), so the longer-than-six-month pattern rests on subgroup confidence intervals rather than a formal difference.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the pooled odds as evidence that concussion itself causes later injury or that persistent deficits are proven, when the review shows only associations and the authors do not measure function or test any assessment tool.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2025,
   "citation":"Liao M, Gu Y, Liu K. The risk of all-cause injury and site-specific injury in athletes after concussion: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Sports Sci Med Rehabil. 2025.",
   "doi":"10.1186/s13102-025-01485-9",
   "abstract":"Objective: to quantify the risk of subsequent all-cause, recurrent concussion, upper-extremity and lower-extremity injury after sport-related concussion. Methods: PRISMA-guided search of five databases for cohort studies through August 2025, scored with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and pooled with random-effects models, with subgroup and meta-regression analyses. Results: 19 cohort studies (86,879 athletes) showed higher odds of all-cause injury (OR 1.93), recurrent concussion (OR 3.06), upper-extremity injury (OR 1.76) and lower-extremity injury (OR 1.49). Risk was significant in studies with follow-up beyond six months and among college athletes, and sport type moderated the all-cause estimate. Conclusion: a concussion history raises later injury risk, and the authors argue for return-to-play protocols that include objective functional assessment.",
   "tldr":"Across 19 cohort studies of more than 86,000 athletes, a prior concussion was associated with roughly twice the odds of a later injury and three times the odds of another concussion. Keep injury monitoring going for well beyond the first months after concussion, but the review does not show which return-to-play test would lower that risk.",
   "methods":"Systematic review and meta-analysis following PRISMA 2020 and registered in PROSPERO, searching PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science and EBSCO for English-language cohort studies. Included studies were scored with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (all 7 to 9 out of 9), adjusted odds ratios were preferred, and random-effects pooling used REML. Subgroup analyses covered country, follow-up duration, design, sport type and athlete level, with meta-regression and leave-one-out sensitivity checks.",
   "findings":"Nineteen cohort studies (86,879 athletes) gave pooled ORs of 1.93 for all-cause injury (95% CI 1.39 to 2.68; I2 = 94.4%), 3.06 for recurrent concussion, 1.76 for upper-extremity injury (two studies) and 1.49 for lower-extremity injury (nine studies). The all-cause estimate was significant in studies with follow-up beyond six months (OR 1.94) and not within six months (OR 1.89, CI 0.91 to 3.94). Sport type was a significant meta-regression moderator (p = 0.038); athlete level and follow-up duration were not (p = 0.130 and p = 0.629). Egger's test gave p = 0.051.",
   "limitations":"Most included studies are observational, five were unadjusted, and heterogeneity was very high, so the pooled estimates are averages across varied settings. The paper's claim that risk persists beyond six months rests on subgroup comparisons, since follow-up duration did not significantly moderate the effect, and the upper-extremity estimate is based on only two studies. The review also restricts to English-language papers and measures injury, not function, so it cannot confirm the authors' conclusion about residual deficits.",
   "practicalImplications":"Flag athletes with a concussion history for injury monitoring, with the highest odds seen after recurrent concussion and for lower-extremity injury. Keep surveillance going beyond the first six months, since pooled odds stayed elevated in longer follow-up studies, and read the all-cause estimate in light of the sport context.",
   "athleteDev":"Use a concussion history as a reason to keep injury monitoring going through the season and beyond. Recurrent concussion carried the largest odds (OR 3.06), and the risk estimate differed by sport type (p = 0.038), so a single pooled risk figure should not be applied to every athlete.",
   "rtp":"The review supports the idea that symptom resolution may not signal full readiness, because elevated injury odds appeared in studies with longer follow-up. It did not test any return-to-play tool or clearance rule, so it cannot say which objective assessment to use or when return is safe."
 }
}

57	Objective: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to quantify the risk
58	 C L
59	 I
60	of subsequent all-cause, recurrent concussion, upper extremity, and lower
61	 T

63	extremity injuries in athletes with a history of sport-related concussion.
64	Methods: Following PRISMA guidelines, cohort studies published from
65	inception through August 2025 were retrieved from PubMed, Cochrane Library,
66	Embase, Web of Science, and EBSCO. The methodological quality of included
67	studies was evaluated using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS). Pooled odds
68	ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using random-
69	effects models. Pre-specified subgroup and meta-regression analyses were
70	conducted to investigate sources of heterogeneity, including injury timing, study
71	design, sport type, and athlete competition level.
72	 1
73	  ARTICLE IN PRESS
74	Results: Nineteen cohort studies involving 86,879 athletes were included.
75	Athletes with a history of concussion had significantly higher odds of
76	sustaining a subsequent all-cause injury (OR=1.93; 95% CI=1.39– 2.68). The
77	risk was most pronounced for recurrent concussion (OR=3.06; 95% CI=1.81–
78	5.17), and was also significantly elevated for upper extremity (OR=1.76; 95%
79	CI=1.10– 2.81) and lower extremity injuries (OR=1.49; 95% CI=1.06– 2.09).
80	Given the high heterogeneity observed in the primary outcomes (I2 > 90%),
81	the pooled effect sizes should be interpreted with caution as average
82	associations across varying study contexts, rather than as precise predictions
83	 S S
84	 E
85	applicable to all settings. Subgroup analysis revealed that injury risk was
86	 PR
87	statistically significant in studies with follow-up periods beyond six months
88	 IN
89	(OR=1.94) but not for shorter durations. The association was strongest and
90	 L E
91	 IC
92	statistically significant among college athletes (OR=2.29; 95% CI=1.53– 3.44),
93	 RT
94	while estimates for professional and high school athletes were not significant.
95	 A
96	Meta-regression identified sport type as a significant moderator of injury risk
97	(p=0.038).
98	Conclusion: A history of concussion significantly increases the risk of
99	subsequent injuries, with the odds being highest for recurrent concussion. The
100	persistence of this risk beyond six months suggests that clinical recovery does
101	not equate to full functional recovery. These findings underscore the need for
102	enhanced return-to-play protocols that incorporate objective functional
103	assessments and targeted rehabilitation to mitigate the heightened vulnerability
104	 2
105	  ARTICLE IN PRESS
106	to injury in post-concussed athletes.
107	Keywords: Concussion; Sports injuries; Upper extremity injury; Lower extremity
108	injury; Athletes; Meta-analysis
109	1. INTRODUCTION
110	Concussion, a form of mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI), is caused by direct
111	or indirect forces to the head, resulting in neurological and cognitive symptoms
112	(Scorza & Cole, 2019). It presents with a range of neurological and cognitive
113	symptoms and has become a major public health issue. In the United States alone,
114	 S S
115	millions of concussions are estimated to occur each year[1]. Systematic reviews and
116	 E
117	 PR
118	meta-analyses have shown that concussion is common across many sports. One study
119	 IN
120	found an overall concussion rate of 0.23 per 1,000 athlete exposures in youth sports,
121	 L E
122	 C
123	with the highest rates seen in high-risk activities such as American football and ice
124	 T I
125	 R
126	hockey [2, 3]. However, actual incidence rates are likely much higher due to
127	 A
128	underreporting and athletes often hiding symptoms[4], further emphasizing the scale of
129	the problem.
130	 Returning to sport too soon after a concussion can increase the risk of further injury.
131	Studies consistently show that athletes with a history of concussion are more likely to
132	experience future musculoskeletal injuries, especially in the lower limbs[5]. This
133	increased risk is thought to result from lasting impairments in balance, proprioception,
134	and neuromuscular control, which may continue even after clinical symptoms have
135	resolved[6, 7]. ‘Clinical recovery,’ as discussed in this study and related literature,
136	is traditionally operationally defined as the resolution of self-reported symptoms
137	 3
138	  ARTICLE IN PRESS
139	and the return of routine clinical physical examination findings to baseline
140	levels[8]. These deficits can reduce an athlete’s ability to coordinate movement, stabilize
141	joints, and maintain posture[9]. The underlying causes likely involve complex changes
142	in how the brain processes sensory and motor signals[10]. Other factors—such as age,
143	sex, and hormone levels—may also influence recovery and risk after repeated
144	concussions[11]. Although these findings point to a link between concussion and later
145	injury, the full extent of the risk, its consistency across athlete populations, and how it
146	affects different body regions remain unclear[12].
147	 Most previous reviews have focused on specific sports or injury types, potentially
148	 S S
149	missing the broader patterns of injury risk among diverse athlete groups[13]. Given the
150	 E
151	 PR
152	growing research and ongoing publication of new studies, an updated and comprehensive
153	 IN
154	meta-analysis is essential. This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to assess the
155	 L E
156	 C
157	overall and site-specific risk of injury in athletes following a concussion. The goal is to
158	 I
159	 RT
160	support better-informed prevention strategies, improve post-concussion care, and guide
161	 A
162	safer return-to-play decisions.
163	2. METHOD
164	This meta-analysis followed the PRISMA 2020[14] guidelines for transparent
165	and standardized reporting. The study protocol was registered in advance with
166	PROSPERO (CRD420251044641) to ensure methodological rigor and
167	transparency.
168	2.1 Data sources and searches
169	A comprehensive and systematic literature search was conducted on August 9,
170	2025, across five major electronic databases: PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane
171	 4
172	  ARTICLE IN PRESS
173	Library, Web of Science, and EBSCO. The search encompassed all literature
174	from the inception of each database through the date of the search. This
175	review was restricted to articles published in the English language.
176	The search strategy was structured around four core concepts to ensure the
177	precise retrieval of relevant studies: (1) exposure (concussion/mild traumatic
178	brain injury); (2) outcome (all types of subsequent injuries); (3) population
179	(athletes); and (4) association (risk).
180	To ensure a comprehensive search, each core concept combined subject
181	headings (e.g., MeSH terms, Emtree) with keywords (i.e., free-text terms). For
182	 S S
183	the exposure concept, search terms included the subject heading "Brain
184	 E
185	 PR
186	Concussion" as well as the keywords "Concussion*," "Commotio Cerebri," and
187	 IN
188	"Mild Traumatic Brain Injury." The outcome concept was searched using the
189	 L E
190	 C
191	subject heading "Wounds and Injuries" and the keywords "Injur*," "Wound*,"
192	 I
193	 RT
194	and "Trauma*." The study population was defined by the subject heading
195	 A
196	"Athletes" and the keyword "Athlete*." To enhance the specificity for
197	epidemiological studies, the association concept utilized the subject heading

805	4.1 Principal findings
806	This meta-analysis, encompassing 19 cohort studies and 86,879 athletes,
807	provides robust evidence that a history of concussion is a significant risk
808	factor for subsequent injuries. Our primary finding reveals that athletes who
809	have sustained a concussion are nearly twice as likely to experience a
810	subsequent all-cause injury compared to their non-concussed counterparts (OR =
811	1.93, 95% CI: 1.39– 2.68). The risk was most pronounced for recurrent
812	concussions, with previously concussed athletes facing a threefold greater odds
813	of sustaining another concussion (OR = 3.06, 95% CI: 1.81– 5.17).
814	 24

Abstract: PR
 IN
 E
Objective: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to quantify the risk
 C L
 I
of subsequent all-cause, recurrent concussion, upper extremity, and lower
 T
 A R
extremity injuries in athletes with a history of sport-related concussion.
Methods: Following PRISMA guidelines, cohort studies published from
inception through August 2025 were retrieved from PubMed, Cochrane Library,
Embase, Web of Science, and EBSCO. The methodological quality of included
studies was evaluated using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS). Pooled odds
ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using random-
effects models. Pre-specified subgroup and meta-regression analyses were
conducted to investigate sources of heterogeneity, including injury timing, study
design, sport type, and athlete competition level.
 1
  ARTICLE IN PRESS
Results: Nineteen cohort studies involving 86,879 athletes were included.
Athletes with a history of concussion had significantly higher odds of
sustaining a subsequent all-cause injury (OR=1.93; 95% CI=1.39– 2.68). The
risk was most pronounced for recurrent concussion (OR=3.06; 95% CI=1.81–
5.17), and was also significantly elevated for upper extremity (OR=1.76; 95%
CI=1.10– 2.81) and lower extremity injuries (OR=1.49; 95% CI=1.06– 2.09).
Given the high heterogeneity observed in the primary outcomes (I2 > 90%),
the pooled effect sizes should be interpreted with caution as average
associations across varying study contexts, rather than as precise predictions
 S S
 E
applicable to all settings. Subgroup analysis revealed that injury risk was
 PR
statistically significant in studies with follow-up periods beyond six months
 IN
(OR=1.94) but not for shorter durations. The association was strongest and
 L E
 IC
statistically significant among college athletes (OR=2.29; 95% CI=1.53– 3.44),
 RT
while estimates for professional and high school athletes were not significant.
 A
Meta-regression identified sport type as a significant moderator of injury risk
(p=0.038).
Conclusion: A history of concussion significantly increases the risk of
subsequent injuries, with the odds being highest for recurrent concussion. The
persistence of this risk beyond six months suggests that clinical recovery does
not equate to full functional recovery. These findings underscore the need for
enhanced return-to-play protocols that incorporate objective functional
assessments and targeted rehabilitation to mitigate the heightened vulnerability
 2
  ARTICLE IN PRESS
to injury in post-concussed athletes.
Keywords: Concussion; Sports injuries; Upper extremity injury; Lower extremity
injury; Athletes; Meta-analysis
1. INTRODUCTION
Concussion, a form of mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI), is caused by direct
or indirect forces to the head, resulting in neurological and cognitive symptoms
(Scorza & Cole, 2019). It presents with a range of neurological and cognitive
symptoms and has become a major public health issue. In the United States alone,
 S S
millions of concussions are estimated to occur each year[1]. Systematic reviews and
 E
 PR
meta-analyses have shown that concussion is common across many sports. One study
 IN
found an overall concussion rate of 0.23 per 1,000 athlete exposures in youth sports,
 L E
 C
with the highest rates seen in high-risk activities such as American football and ice
 T I
 R
hockey [2, 3]. However, actual incidence rates are likely much higher due to
 A
underreporting and athletes often hiding symptoms[4], further emphasizing the scale of
the problem.
 Returning to sport too soon after a concussion can increase the risk of further injury.
Studies consistently show that athletes with a history of concussion are more likely to
experience future musculoskeletal injuries, especially in the lower limbs[5]. This
increased risk is thought to result from lasting impairments in balance, proprioception,
and neuromuscular control, which may continue even after clinical symptoms have
resolved[6, 7]. ‘Clinical recovery,’ as discussed in this study and related literature,
is traditionally operationally defined as the resolution of self-reported symptoms
 3
  ARTICLE IN PRESS
and the return of routine clinical physical examination findings to baseline
levels[8]. These deficits can reduce an athlete’s ability to coordinate movement, stabilize
joints, and maintain posture[9]. The underlying causes likely involve complex changes
in how the brain processes sensory and motor signals[10]. Other factors—such as age,
sex, and hormone levels—may also influence recovery and risk after repeated
concussions[11]. Although these findings point to a link between concussion and later
injury, the full extent of the risk, its consistency across athlete populations, and how it
affects different body regions remain unclear[12].
 Most previous reviews have focused on specific sports or injury types, potentially
 S S
missing the broader patterns of injury risk among diverse athlete groups[13]. Given the
 E
 PR
growing research and ongoing publication of new studies, an updated and comprehensive
 IN
meta-analysis is essential. This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to assess the
 L E
 C
overall and site-specific risk of injury in athletes following a concussion. The goal is to
 I
 RT
support better-informed prevention strategies, improve post-concussion care, and guide
 A
safer return-to-play decisions.
2. METHOD
This meta-analysis followed the PRISMA 2020[14] guidelines for transparent
and standardized reporting. The study protocol was registered in advance with
PROSPERO (CRD420251044641) to ensure methodological rigor and
transparency.
2.1 Data sources and searches
A comprehensive and systematic literature search was conducted on August 9,
2025, across five major electronic databases: PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane
 4
  ARTICLE IN PRESS
Library, Web of Science, and EBSCO. The search encompassed all literature
from the inception of each database through the date of the search. This
review was restricted to articles published in the English language.
The search strategy was structured around four core concepts to ensure the
precise retrieval of relevant studies: (1) exposure (concussion/mild traumatic
brain injury); (2) outcome (all types of subsequent injuries); (3) population
(athletes); and (4) association (risk).
To ensure a comprehensive search, each core concept combined subject
headings (e.g., MeSH terms, Emtree) with keywords (i.e., free-text terms). For
 S S
the exposure concept, search terms included the subject heading "Brain
 E
 PR
Concussion" as well as the keywords "Concussion*," "Commotio Cerebri," and
 IN
"Mild Traumatic Brain Injury." The outcome concept was searched using the
 L E
 C
subject heading "Wounds and Injuries" and the keywords "Injur*," "Wound*,"
 I
 RT
and "Trauma*." The study population was defined by the subject heading
 A
"Athletes" and the keyword "Athlete*." To enhance the specificity for
epidemiological studies, the association concept utilized the subject heading
"Risk" and the keyword "Risk*."
Within each conceptual group, the respective search terms were combined using
the Boolean operator "OR." Subsequently, the four core concepts were
combined using the "AND" operator. The complete, detailed search strategies
for all five databases are available in the supplementary materials
(Supplementary Table S1, S2, S3, S4 and S5). In addition, a rigorous manual
 5
  ARTICLE IN PRESS
search of the reference lists of all included studies and relevant systematic
reviews was performed to identify any potentially eligible articles that may
have been missed.
2.2 Eligibility criteria
Studies meeting the following criteria were eligible for inclusion: (1) Study
Design: The investigation must be a retrospective or prospective cohort study.
(2) Participants and Exposure: The study population must consist of athletes,
with the exposure of interest being a history of concussion. (3) Outcomes: The
study assessed the risk of subsequent injury. The primary outcome was defined
 S S
as "all-cause injury," encompassing all new injuries sustained during sports
 E
 PR
participation, including acute/overuse and contact/non-contact injuries, while
 IN
explicitly excluding non-sport-related illnesses and general medical conditions.
 L E
 C
Secondary outcomes included recurrent concussion, upper extremity injury, and
 I
 RT
lower extremity injury. (4) Data Reporting: To be included, a study must have
 A
reported effect estimates— such as an odds ratio (OR), relative risk (RR), or
hazard ratio (HR)—with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the
association between concussion and the specified injury outcomes, or provided
sufficient raw data to calculate these metrics. Exclusion criteria comprised
conference abstracts, narrative reviews, meta-analyses, study protocols, and case
reports. To address potential data overlap in studies utilizing the same database
(e.g., NCAA, NFL), priority was given to the publication with the largest
sample size or longest follow-up period to prevent statistical bias. Finally,
 6
  ARTICLE IN PRESS
studies that did not report relevant outcomes or lacked extractable data for
effect size calculation were excluded.
2.3 Study selection
Two reviewers (MYL and YG) independently screened studies based on
predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. The process began with a review of
titles and abstracts to exclude duplicates and clearly irrelevant studies. Full
texts of potentially eligible articles were then assessed to confirm final
eligibility. Disagreements were resolved through consultation with a third
reviewer (KYL) to reach consensus.
2.4 Risk of bias
 S S
 E
 PR
The methodological quality of each included cohort study was evaluated using the
 IN
Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS)[15]. This scale assesses three key areas: participant
 L E
 C
selection and exposure assessment (maximum of 4 points), comparability between study
 T I
 R
groups (maximum of 2 points), and outcome assessment along with adequacy of follow-
 A
up (maximum of 3 points). Based on the total score, studies were categorized as low
quality (0–3 points), moderate quality (4–6 points), or high quality (7–9 points).A total
of 19 cohort studies were included in this analysis. The detailed NOS scores for
each study are presented in (Supplementary Table S6). All included studies
scored between 7 and 9 points, and were consequently judged to be of high
methodological quality, indicating a low overall risk of bias.
2.5 Statistical analysis
All statistical analyses for this systematic review and meta-analysis were
performed using R (v4.4.1 or later), primarily with the metafor, forestplot,
 7
  ARTICLE IN PRESS
dplyr, and ggplot2 packages.
2.5.1 Effect Size Calculation and Pooling
The primary effect measure was the odds ratio (OR). To minimize confounding
bias, priority was given to adjusted odds ratios (aORs) derived from
multivariate regression analyses or matched designs[16]; if adjusted results were
not reported, unadjusted ORs were utilized. For all models, the natural
logarithm of the OR (log-OR) and its corresponding standard error (SE) were
used as inputs from each individual study. We employed a random-effects
model to pool the data, utilizing the restricted maximum-likelihood (REML)
 S S
estimator, which is recommended for its robust performance in meta-regression.
 E
 PR
The contribution of each study to the pooled estimate was weighted using the
 IN
inverse-variance method. All results are presented as ORs with their 95%
 L E
 C
confidence intervals (CIs). Statistical significance was defined as a p-value <
 I
0.05.
 RT
 A
2.5.2 Assessment of Heterogeneity and Model Variance
Between-study heterogeneity was assessed using Cochrane's Q statistic and
quantified with the I ² statistic. I ² values were interpreted as follows: ≤25%
(low), 25–75% (moderate), and >75% (high). For meta-regression models, the
adjusted R ² statistic was reported to quantify the proportion of heterogeneity
explained by the included moderators.
2.5.3 Assessment of Publication Bias and Sensitivity Analysis
The potential for publication bias was evaluated through visual inspection of
funnel plots and formally tested using Egger’s linear regression, where a p-
 8
  ARTICLE IN PRESS
value > 0.05 was considered indicative of no significant publication bias. To
assess the robustness of the results, leave-one-out sensitivity analyses were
conducted.
2.5.4 Subgroup and Meta-Regression Analyses
To investigate potential sources of heterogeneity, pre-specified subgroup
analyses were conducted based on the following moderators: athlete level
(Professional, College, High School), country (USA, Australia, Denmark,
Germany, UK), research design (Prospective Cohort, Retrospective Cohort),
follow-up duration (Beyond 6 months, Within 6 months) and sport type
 S S
(Contact sports, Both contact and non-contact). The statistical significance of
 E
 PR
differences between subgroups was tested using random-effects meta-regression
 IN
(p < 0.05). For each categorical moderator, we performed a meta-regression
 L E
 C
analysis that included an interaction term with study precision (1/SE) to
 T I
 R
explore variations in effect size across subgroups. Results were visualized using
 A
stratified meta-regression plots and subgroup forest plots. All analytical
procedures strictly adhered to the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, and the statistical
methods were reviewed by a biostatistician to ensure methodological rigor and
accuracy.
3. RESULTS
3.1 Literature search
This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted across five major
databases: PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and

"brain concussion" [MeSH Terms], "mild traumatic brain injury") and
subsequent injuries (e.g., "wounds and injuries" [MeSH Terms], "injur*").
The initial search yielded a total of 5,716 records. After the removal of 1,036
duplicates through both automated and manual processes, the titles and
abstracts of the remaining 4,680 articles were screened, from which 4,489 were
excluded for being clearly irrelevant to the topic. Subsequently, the full texts
of the 191 potentially relevant papers were retrieved and reviewed to assess
their final eligibility. Following a rigorous evaluation based on predefined

inclusion and exclusion criteria, 19 studies met the criteria and were ultimately

included in this meta-analysis. A detailed flowchart of the study selection
process is presented in Figure 1. IN

3.3 Risk of All-Cause Injury associated with history of concussion
Nineteen cohort studies were included to assess the link between a history of concussion
and the risk of subsequent all-cause Injury[17-35]. Substantial heterogeneity was
observed across studies (I² = 94.4%, p < 0.001), prompting the use of a random-effects

faced a significantly higher risk of later injury compared to those without (OR = 1.93,
95% CI: 1.39–2.68; p < 0.001) (Figure 2). This suggests that a prior concussion may
be associated with an approximately 93% increased risk of sustaining a subsequent
sports-related injury.

To assess the robustness of the pooled estimates, a leave-one-out sensitivity
analysis was conducted for each of the four primary outcomes: all-cause injury,
upper extremity injury, lower extremity injury, and recurrent concussion. This

recalculating the overall effect size for the remaining studies.

outcomes. The removal of any single study did not result in a meaningful
change to the pooled odds ratios, nor did it alter the statistical significance of

4.DISCUSSIONRT
 A
4.1 Principal findings
This meta-analysis, encompassing 19 cohort studies and 86,879 athletes,
provides robust evidence that a history of concussion is a significant risk
factor for subsequent injuries. Our primary finding reveals that athletes who
have sustained a concussion are nearly twice as likely to experience a
subsequent all-cause injury compared to their non-concussed counterparts (OR =
1.93, 95% CI: 1.39– 2.68). The risk was most pronounced for recurrent
concussions, with previously concussed athletes facing a threefold greater odds
of sustaining another concussion (OR = 3.06, 95% CI: 1.81– 5.17).
 24
  ARTICLE IN PRESS
Furthermore, the risk extended to other body regions, with significantly
elevated odds for both upper extremity (OR = 1.76, 95% CI: 1.10–2.81) and
lower extremity injuries (OR = 1.49, 95% CI: 1.06–2.09).
4.2 Comparison with Prior Evidence and Novel Insights
The principal findings of this meta-analysis are consistent with and build upon
the existing body of literature, strengthening the evidence base for the
association between concussion and subsequent injury risk. Our pooled estimate
for all-cause injury (OR=1.93) aligns remarkably well with the landmark meta-
analysis by Mcpherson et al (2019)[36], which reported that concussed athletes
 S S
had over two times greater odds of sustaining a subsequent musculoskeletal injury
 E
 PR
(MSKI) (OR=2.11). Similarly, our finding of a 49% increased risk for lower
 IN
extremity injury (OR=1.49) is comparable to other recent systematic reviews. For
 L E
 C
instance, Jildeh et al (2022)[37] reported an odds ratio of 1.85 for LE injury
 I
 RT
within one year of concussion, and Mccann et al (2022b)[38] found a 58% greater
 A
risk (RR=1.58) specifically in college athletes. Furthermore, the threefold
increased risk for recurrent concussion (OR=3.06) strongly corroborates the well-
established principle that a prior concussion is the single greatest predictor for a
future one [39]. This estimate is quantitatively similar to the findings of van Ierssel
et al (2021)[40], who reported a pooled risk ratio of 3.64 for recurrent
concussion in children and adolescents.
 Beyond corroborating previous work, the present study offers several novel
insights derived from our detailed subgroup and meta-regression analyses. A
 25
  ARTICLE IN PRESS
key new finding is the identification of sport type as a significant moderator
of all-cause injury risk (meta-regression p=0.038). This suggests that the risk
profile for athletes in contact sports may differ from that of athletes in cohorts
that include participants from non-contact sports, potentially reflecting
differences in exposure to high-impact forces or sport-specific movement
patterns. Our subgroup analysis also revealed a nuanced picture across
competition levels. The risk was most pronounced and statistically significant
among college athletes (OR=2.29), whereas the estimates for professional
(OR=1.40) and high school athletes (OR=2.03) did not reach statistical
 S S
 E
significance. This heterogeneity in findings across levels is not a contradiction
 PR
but a critical insight. The strong signal in collegiate sports may be attributable
 IN
to the high-quality, systematic injury surveillance systems common in large
 L E
 IC
NCAA programs, which reduce measurement error and increase statistical
 RT
power. Conversely, the non-significant finding in professional athletes could be
 A
multifactorial, stemming from superior, individualized rehabilitation, a "survivor
bias" where only the most robust athletes compete [41], or smaller study
sample sizes. At the high school level, the lack of statistical significance is
likely due to methodological noise, as inconsistent injury reporting and high
variability in athlete maturation and care introduce significant heterogeneity (I2
=94.4%), obscuring a clear statistical signal.
 The study also explored how injury risk evolves over time. While prior work
suggested increased risk within 90 days [42] , our analysis indicates that the
 26
  ARTICLE IN PRESS
increase in risk was statistically significant in studies with follow-up periods
exceeding six months (OR=1.94), whereas the association did not reach
statistical significance in studies with shorter follow-up durations (<6 months;
p=0.087). It is important to note that this is an observational finding. It
suggests that within existing cohort studies, susceptibility to injury following
concussion may not resolve immediately upon the cessation of short-term
clinical symptoms, but rather remains observable over a more extended
temporal window. This implies that the underlying neuromuscular deficits
driving this elevated risk are not transient but persistent, manifesting as injuries
 S S
 E
during prolonged athletic exposure, thereby challenging the traditional notion of
 PR
"rapid recovery." The prevailing hypothesis regarding the mechanism of this
 IN
increased risk is that subtle, sub-clinical neurological deficits persist in athletes
 L E
 IC
even after they are clinically deemed "recovered" following symptom resolution
 RT
and standard return-to-play assessments [43]. These deficits include impaired
 A
neuromuscular and postural control, where concussion disrupts the brain's
processing of visual, vestibular, and somatosensory information, leading to
altered gait, diminished stability, and delayed reaction times [44]. Given that
traditional clinical evaluations often fail to detect these subtle functional
impairments, the Amsterdam International Consensus Statement and recent
studies strongly advocate for the implementation of objective, standardized
assessment tools [45]. For instance, the ImPACT test can be utilized to detect
delays in cognitive reaction time, while the Sway or Balance Error Scoring
 27
  ARTICLE IN PRESS
System (BESS) serves to assess postural stability [46, 47]. Relying solely on
symptom resolution without validation from these objective tools may fail to
identify latent neuromuscular deficits that are sufficient to increase the risk of
subsequent injury. Furthermore, altered sensorimotor integration and cognitive
deficits may leave athletes with insufficient cognitive resources to maintain
proper movement mechanics during complex competitive scenarios, thereby
exacerbating injury risk [48].
4.3 Clinical and Preventive Implications
Recovery from concussion often extends beyond the resolution of symptoms, with
 S S
ongoing neuromuscular and balance deficits that increase the risk of re-injury[49, 50].
 E
 PR
These findings support extending post-concussion monitoring beyond six months and
 IN
adopting individualized rehabilitation plans focused on restoring motor control, balance,
 L E
 C
and cognitive-motor integration[6, 51, 52]. High-risk groups—especially professional
 I
 RT
athletes—may benefit from interventions such as biomechanical screening and
 A
neurocognitive-motor training[53, 54]. Comprehensive assessment strategies that
include physical, cognitive, and psychosocial evaluations can guide more effective
treatment plans[55]. Recent evidence also suggests that early reintroduction of physical
activity, rather than prolonged rest, may promote faster recovery[56, 57]. Proven
approaches include aerobic exercise[58], cognitive rehabilitation, and vestibular
therapy[59]. Return-to-play (RTP) decisions should account for the increased risk of
MSK injury[60]. Incorporating neuromechanical assessments into RTP protocols can
help ensure athletes are physically ready to resume competition. Ongoing injury
 28
  ARTICLE IN PRESS
surveillance—particularly in contact sports—along with educational programs
promoting symptom reporting, is essential to preventing reinjury and addressing
underreporting of concussion[61].
5. STRENGTHS, LIMITATIONS, AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS
The credibility of this meta-analysis is supported by several methodological
strengths. The study was conducted in strict adherence to the PRISMA 2020
guidelines and was pre-registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251044641),
ensuring methodological transparency and minimizing the risk of reporting bias.
A comprehensive search strategy was executed across five major electronic
 S S
databases, supplemented by manual reference checks, to ensure a thorough and
 E
 PR
representative sample of the available literature. The inclusion of 19 cohort
 IN
studies with a large pooled sample of 86,879 athletes provides substantial
 L E
 C
statistical power and enhances the generalizability of the findings. Furthermore,
 I
 RT
we employed robust statistical methods, including a random-effects model
 A
appropriate for heterogeneous data, and conducted leave-one-out sensitivity
analyses that confirmed the stability of our results. Crucially, by using
subgroup and meta-regression analyses, this study moved beyond a simple
pooled estimate to actively investigate potential sources of heterogeneity.
Finally, formal testing with Egger’ s regression ( p=0.051) and visual
inspection of the funnel plot revealed no significant evidence of publication
bias, further strengthening confidence in the results.
 Despite the aforementioned strengths, several limitations must be
 29
  ARTICLE IN PRESS
acknowledged. First, a high degree of statistical heterogeneity was observed in
the analysis of all-cause injury (I2 = 94.4%). Although meta-regression
identified sport type as a significant moderator, residual heterogeneity suggests
that the pooled effect sizes should be interpreted as average associations across
varying study contexts, rather than as uniform predictive values applicable to
all settings. Second, while nearly three-quarters (73.7%) of the included studies
adjusted for critical confounders such as prior injury history— and sensitivity
analyses confirmed the stability of the results— the inclusion of unadjusted
studies (n=5) and inconsistencies in covariate selection across studies may still
 S S
 E
introduce potential bias. Third, the robustness of evidence for certain subgroups
 PR
is limited; the assessment of upper extremity injury was based on only two
 IN
studies, and the lack of significant risk observed in professional and high
 L E
 IC
school athlete subgroups is more likely attributable to insufficient statistical
 RT
power or methodological discrepancies rather than an absence of risk; thus, it
 A
should not be inferred that these populations are risk-free. Finally, heterogeneity
in the definitions of "concussion" and "injury," potential unmeasured
confounders, and language bias resulting from restricting the search to English-
language literature may affect the precision of the effect estimates. Future research
should prioritize large-scale, multinational, prospective cohort studies utilizing
standardized definitions to further elucidate causal relationships and optimize
prevention strategies.
6.CONCLUSION
 30
  ARTICLE IN PRESS
In conclusion, this systematic review and meta-analysis provides robust
evidence that athletes with a history of concussion face a significantly elevated
risk of sustaining various subsequent injuries. The findings explicitly indicate
that symptom resolution does not equate to full functional recovery. Although
athletes may appear symptom-free, objective assessment tools— such as the
ImPACT or Sway tests— may reveal persistent neuromuscular deficits that do
not fully resolve despite the cessation of reported symptoms. Consequently,
relying solely on symptom clearance as the benchmark for "clinical recovery"
may fail to accurately reflect an athlete's true functional status. A window of
 S S
 E
heightened vulnerability to injury persists for a prolonged period after athletes
 PR
are cleared to return to play under current standard protocols. Accordingly,
 IN
these results support the refinement of existing concussion management
 L E
 IC
protocols, particularly the integration of scientifically validated, objective
 RT
functional assessments, to ensure full recovery prior to return-to-play and to
 A
mitigate the risk of subsequent injury. Adopting such a comprehensive strategy
is essential for safeguarding the short- and long-term health of athletes.

{
 "id":"Q37",
 "sourceFile":"The role of a short nap in improving cognitive motor and sprint performance in participants with partial sleep deprivation.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Text title 'The role of a short post-lunch nap in improving cognitive, motor, and sprint performance in participants with partial sleep deprivation' matches the filename apart from the omitted 'post-lunch' and punctuation.",
 "confidence":"medium",
 "studyDesign":"Laboratory / Experimental Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Recovery & Readiness",
 "domains":["Recovery & Readiness","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Coaching","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Crossover laboratory study of 10 healthy young men (mean age 23.3) who slept 4 hours less than usual, then either napped for 30 minutes at 13:00 or sat quietly, with testing 30 minutes later. The nap improved alertness, reduced sleepiness, improved digit-span memory and lowered heart rate and temperature. Mean 2 m and 20 m sprint times were faster after the nap (20 m fell from 3.971 s to 3.878 s), while reaction-time means and grip strength were not changed.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The sample is 10 healthy young men who were not described as athletes, so the sprint results are from a non-athlete group. The study uses a single nap length, two short sprint distances, subjective sleep measures and no objective sleep recording, so the findings do not show benefit for longer events or for athletes' real training schedules.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the sprint improvement as a proven performance benefit for athletes who are short on sleep, when it is a small, short-distance result from 10 non-athletes in a single laboratory session.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2007,
   "citation":"Waterhouse J, Atkinson G, Edwards B, Reilly T. The role of a short post-lunch nap in improving cognitive, motor, and sprint performance in participants with partial sleep deprivation. J Sports Sci. 2007;25(14):1557-1566.",
   "doi":"10.1080/02640410701244983",
   "abstract":"The study tested whether a 30-minute post-lunch nap improves alertness and performance after a night of shortened sleep. Ten healthy males either napped or sat quietly from 13:00 to 13:30 after 3 hours of sleep. Alertness, short-term memory, heart rate, temperature, reaction time, grip strength and 2 m and 20 m sprint times were measured 30 minutes later. The nap improved alertness, sleepiness, short-term memory, 8-choice reaction accuracy and sprint times, but not mean reaction times or grip strength.",
   "tldr":"In 10 healthy young men with one night of shortened sleep, a 30-minute afternoon nap improved alertness, memory and short-sprint times compared with quiet rest. The study is small and used non-athletes, so it suggests a possible benefit for athletes but does not prove it.",
   "methods":"Crossover laboratory study of 10 healthy males (mean age 23.3 years) who slept 4 hours less than usual the night before testing. In the nap condition they rested in bed from 13:00 to 13:30; in the control they read quietly. Thirty minutes later they completed alertness and sleepiness scales, a digit-span memory test, an 8-choice reaction time test, handgrip strength and three 2 m and 20 m sprints, with heart rate and aural temperature recorded.",
   "findings":"The nap lowered heart rate and aural temperature and improved subjective alertness (t9 = 5.77, p < .001) and sleepiness (t9 = 6.74, p < .001). Digit-span memory improved after the nap (nap main effect F = 9.5, p = .013). Mean reaction times and grip strength were not affected. Sprint times were faster after the nap, with the 2 m mean falling from 1.060 s to 1.019 s (p = .031) and the 20 m mean from 3.971 s to 3.878 s (p = .013), with the sprint results reported as the authors summarise them.",
   "limitations":"The study had 10 male participants, none described as athletes, and tested only one nap length at one time of day. Sleep was not measured objectively, and the sprint results come from three trials at 2 m and 20 m, so they cannot be extended to longer events; the authors also note that a warm-up effect may explain part of the sprint change. The 8-choice error difference was only marginally significant (p = .070), and some of the within-study correlations were not significant.",
   "practicalImplications":"A 30-minute lunchtime nap after restricted sleep may improve alertness and short-sprint times in healthy adults, so it is worth trialling for athletes who lose sleep. Do not expect the same effect on mean reaction time or grip strength, which were unchanged, and do not expect it at longer distances.",
   "athleteDev":"A short afternoon nap could be tested as a readiness tactic on days after restricted sleep, with sprint times and alertness checked against a no-nap day. The result comes from non-athletes, so the effect should be confirmed in the squad before it becomes routine.",
   "rtp":"The study does not address injured athletes or return to sport and cannot be used to judge return-to-sport readiness."
 }
}

Journal of Sports Sciences, December 2007; 25(14): 1557 – 1566
The role of a short post-lunch nap in improving cognitive, motor,
and sprint performance in participants with partial sleep deprivation
J. WATERHOUSE, G. ATKINSON, B. EDWARDS, & T. REILLY
Research Institute for Sport and Exercise Sciences, Liverpool John Moores University, Liverpool, UK
(Accepted 26 January 2007)
Abstract
The aim of this study was to determine the effects of a post-lunch nap on subjective alertness and performance following
partial sleep loss. Ten healthy males (mean age 23.3 years, s ¼ 3.4) either napped or sat quietly from 13:00 to 13:30 h after a
night of shortened sleep (sleep 23:00 – 03:00 h only). Thirty minutes after the afternoon nap or control (no-nap) condition,
alertness, short-term memory, intra-aural temperature, heart rate, choice reaction time, grip strength, and times for 2-m and
20-m sprints were recorded. The afternoon nap lowered heart rate and intra-aural temperature. Alertness, sleepiness, short-
term memory, and accuracy at the 8-choice reaction time test were improved by napping (P 5 0.05), but mean reaction
times and grip strength were not affected (P 4 0.05). Sprint times were improved. Mean time for the 2-m sprints fell from
1.060 s (sx ¼ 0.018) to 1.019 s (sx ¼ 0.019) (P ¼ 0.031 paired t-test); mean time for the 20-m sprints fell from 3.971 s
(sx ¼ 0.054) to 3.878 s (sx ¼ 0.047) (P ¼ 0.013). These results indicate that a post-lunch nap improves alertness and aspects
of mental and physical performance following partial sleep loss, and have implications for athletes with restricted sleep during
training or before competition.
